about: How Asset Studio (and Evani.commons) picks each procedural asset's reference target: the reference CLASS, the framing per class and category, and for things that can't be photographed the test scene and measurable behaviour spec. Which class an asset is in lives in catalog/procedural/library.json: `ref_class` on each category (its default) and on an asset only where it differs. This file holds what each class means. tools/procedural/gen_ref_classes.mjs checks both, writes the tab's table (tools/evani-commons-tab/classes.js) and the table in docs/ASSET_STUDIO_GUIDE.md ('Reference classes'). Materials (catalog/materials) are always class object. Layering (the pre-loaded prompts plan): style -> type -> category -> item; the class and the category framing sit at the category layer, an asset's own `show`/`time`/`camera` at the item layer. Owner's decision 2026-11-06: environment and atmosphere are judged from the player's camera; wind and other things you can't photograph are judged by their effect on a standard test scene plus measured checks. Viewpoints (owner's decision 2026-11-06, Canyons first): a reference carries a list of viewpoints (`viewpoints` below); every asset has its class's one default view unless its entry in `assets` gives `views` and a `layout`. A multi-view asset has ONE reference picture with every view as a panel of the same landform (the `layouts` template), the author's capture is the matching panel picture, and the reviewer scores that one combined comparison with notes per view and one score. `view_audit` holds the reason for each asset's views and the suggestions waiting for the owner; only `views` in `assets` is in force.

object.label: Standalone object or material
object.reference: Studio still: the whole object in frame, three-quarter view, neutral grey backdrop, soft key light.
object.template: {lead} {what}, whole object in frame, three-quarter view, neutral grey backdrop, soft key light, no text. {style} reference for a 3D {kind}.
review: Judge it as an object: silhouette and proportions, scale of detail, colour and value, roughness and sheen, wear, chips and cracks as real geometry, and the light and contact shadow match.
The capture must be framed and lit like the reference's studio view.

scene.label: Environment or atmosphere, seen from the player's camera
scene.reference: A still from a ground-level player camera in the scene, in context: set camera height, field of view, horizon placement and time of day; no studio, no backdrop.
scene.template: {lead} {what}: {show}. Camera at a standing player's eye height (1.7 m) on the ground, level, {fov} degree horizontal field of view, horizon {horizon}. {time}. Natural light, everything at game scale and in its place in the world; no studio, no backdrop, no object on a table, no frame, no people, no text. {style} reference for a 3D game's procedural environment, as the player sees it.
review: Judge it as seen from the game camera, not as an object: the capture must use the reference's eye-height camera, field of view and horizon line (say if it does not, and judge what you can).

Score the SUBJECT (the SUBJECT line at the top of the brief and of each request) as the player reads it at game scale: its placement against the horizon, its colour and value gradient, aerial perspective and haze with distance, the light direction and time of day, and its look at near, middle and far distance.

The subject's detail scale per metre must be right for a standing player (for example grass blades for a grass asset, rock faces for rocks, wave crests for water, cloud edges and disc sizes at their real angular size for sky).

Everything named CONTEXT ONLY is background: it never lowers the score and never becomes a 'wrong' line or a fix item; mention it at most once, as background. Measure only inside the subject's judge region.
A capture framed as a studio object (the asset alone on a backdrop, seen from outside) scores at most 2, however good its surface.
measure: horizon height in the frame (fraction from the bottom)
mean and spread of luminance and colour inside the subject's judge region (for sky items: the sky above the horizon line only)
the contrast drop from near to far (aerial perspective) where the subject spans distance
for sky items: the colour at the horizon and at the top of the frame, and the sun or moon disc's size in pixels and degrees

behaviour.label: Behaviour you can't photograph (forces and motion-only effects)
behaviour.reference: A standard proxy test scene shown as a short motion reference (a sheet of four frames 0.5 s apart from one fixed camera) plus a measurable behaviour spec.
behaviour.template: {lead} sheet of four frames in a 2 by 2 grid, 0.5 s apart, from one fixed camera at eye height, showing {what} only through its effect on a standard test scene: {scene}. {cues}. The same framing in all four frames, natural daylight, no arrows, no labels, no text. Motion reference for a 3D game's procedural effect.
review: Score the effect, not a picture of the thing: the author's capture is the same test scene (four frames 0.5 s apart from the same camera) plus measured values from the engine's live params or telemetry.

Check every line of the behaviour spec: the measured value against its range (pass or fail), and on the frames that the motion shows it (a sway amplitude you can see between frames, a gust front crossing the field, directions that agree).

Scoring: all checks pass and the motion reads natural in the frames: 4.5 or more; at least three quarters pass: up to 4; half to three quarters: up to 3; under half: at most 2.5; no measured values at all: at most 2.
Name each check with its measured value and pass or fail in 'wrong' or 'summary'.

staged.show: a strip of flat, featureless mid-grey ground along the bottom quarter of the frame running to the horizon, with plain matte mid-grey boxes and square pillars standing on it for scale: a near pair of 1 m cubes about 12 m away, left and right of centre; a middle pair of 8 m tall pillars about 60 m away; and a far line of tall 40 m pillars from about 300 m out to 1.5 km along the horizon. staged.focus: the cloud layers only: how many decks and at what heights (far above the tallest pillars), each deck's coverage, gaps and texture (broken rolls below, a thin even veil above), their flat, level, darker bases, their colour and sunlit edges, and how they recede in perspective toward the horizon
staged.subject: the cloud layers only: the decks' number and heights above the pillars, each deck's coverage, gaps and texture, their flat, level bases and shading, their colour against the sky, and how they shrink and crowd together toward the horizon
staged.context: the grey blocks, pillars and ground, and the plain sky behind the clouds: neutral staging placed only to show the cloud layers and their scale; their shape, number, placement, material and edges are never scored
staged.compare: Compare the cloud decks against the pillars and the horizon: their height far above the tallest pillars, how many layers there are and how they overlap, how much of the sky each covers and the size of its gaps, the flat, level bases and their shading, their colour and value against the blue, and how their rolls shrink and crowd together toward the horizon (their perspective falloff).

subjects.about: What each column is judged on (Chris, 2026-11-08: "the purpose of the Sun and moon disc is to deliver a sky asset, not grass"; column 38 drifted to the foreground meadow because nothing named the asset's own part of the picture). Every column gets one SUBJECT line (scored and fixed) and one CONTEXT ONLY line (background: never lowers the score, never a fix item) in every launch and message, and a judge region that the tab's own measurements use (metrics.js). Layering: the class's default, then the category's, then the asset's own; {name} is the asset's name. Regions: whole (the whole picture), above-horizon (the rows above the reference's horizon line), below-horizon (the rows below it). Checked and copied into the tab by tools/procedural/gen_ref_classes.mjs.

above-horizon.label: the sky above the horizon line

below-horizon.label: the ground below the horizon line

object.subject: the {name} itself: its shape, proportions, surface, material, wear, and its light and contact shadow
object.context: the backdrop, the floor and the studio set-up

scene.subject: the {name} as the player sees it, wherever it is in the frame
scene.context: anything in the frame that is not the {name} (other landforms, plants, sky or props placed for context)

behaviour.subject: the {name}'s effect on the test scene (its motion between the frames) and every measured spec value
behaviour.context: the test scene's own props and surfaces (how the grass, trees, flag, water or body are modelled)

material.subject: the {name} material itself: its pattern, colour and value, roughness and sheen, relief and wear, at its real scale
material.context: the sample's shape, the backdrop and the studio set-up

sky.subject: the {name} and the sky above the horizon line: its shape, size, colour and light, the sky's gradient from horizon to zenith, and the haze and scattering along the horizon
sky.context: the ground, fields, grass, trees and hills below the horizon: they only place the horizon and take the light; never score or fix them

terrain.subject: the {name} landform: its shape and scale, its surfaces near to far, and how it sits in the land
terrain.context: the sky, clouds and any plants or props placed on it

water.subject: the {name}: the water's surface, colour, transparency, reflections, motion cues and its edge
water.context: the sky and the land, plants and props around it

roads.subject: the {name}: its surface, edges, markings and how it runs through the ground
roads.context: the sky, the verges' plants, and buildings and props beside it

vegetation.subject: the {name}: the plants themselves (blades, leaves, stems), their density, clumping and colour, and how they cover the ground near to far
vegetation.context: the sky, trees and landforms behind them

trees.subject: the {name}: trunks, branches, canopy and leaves, their shape, density and light
trees.context: the sky, the ground cover and the landforms around them

rocks.subject: the {name}: the rock forms, their faces, cracks and colour, and how they sit on the ground
rocks.context: the sky, plants and landforms around them

agriculture.subject: the {name}: the crops or works, their rows, plants and structure
agriculture.context: the sky, the hedges and trees at the field's edge, and the landforms around them

sky-sun-and-moon-discs.subject: the sun and moon discs and the sky around them: disc shape and true angular size, limb darkening, the white core, glow, halo, aureole and bloom, the moon's crescent and phase, the sky gradient from horizon to zenith, and the scattering and haze colour along the horizon

sky-dynamic-sky-dome.subject: the sky dome above the horizon line: its colour and value gradient from horizon to zenith, the sun's glow, the haze along the horizon and the clouds' place in it

sky-distance-fog.subject: the fog: how the land and objects fade into it with distance, its colour, density and height
sky-distance-fog.context: how the hedges, trees and hills themselves are modelled (only their fading counts)

sky-ground-mist.subject: the mist layer: its height and thickness, how it thins upwards and lies over the ground and between the trees
sky-ground-mist.context: how the meadow and trees themselves are modelled (only the mist over them counts)

sky-rain.subject: the rain: the streaks, their density, angle and depth, the wet sheen and the rings in puddles
sky-rain.context: how the lane, fields and trees themselves are modelled (only the rain and the wetness on them count)

sky-snowfall.subject: the snowfall: flakes near and far, their size, density and motion cues, and the fresh cover
sky-snowfall.context: how the field and trees themselves are modelled (only the snow on them counts)

sky-hail.subject: the hail: the falling stones, their size and density, and the stones bouncing and lying on the ground
sky-hail.context: how the field and path themselves are modelled (only the hail on them counts)

sky-dust-storms.subject: the dust: the rolling wall, its colour and density, how it hides the distance and dims the sun
sky-dust-storms.context: how the dry land itself is modelled (only the dust over it counts)

sky-sandstorms.subject: the blowing sand: the streams off the crests, the thick ochre air and the dimmed sun
sky-sandstorms.context: how the dunes themselves are modelled (only the sand in the air counts)

sky-lightning.subject: the lightning bolt and the storm cloud it comes from, lit from inside
sky-lightning.context: how the open country under it is modelled

sky-rainbows.subject: the rainbow arc and the shower behind it: its colours, width and brightness, and the darker sky outside it
sky-rainbows.context: how the fields under it are modelled

sky-aurora-effects.subject: the aurora curtains and the starry sky above the horizon: their colour, folds, motion cues and brightness
sky-aurora-effects.context: the snowy landscape below the horizon

two-panel.label: two panels side by side
two-panel.template: {lead} {what}: one image made of two panels side by side, split down the middle by a thin dark line, each panel half the width. Left panel: {left}. Right panel: {right}. Both panels show the same {name}, with the same features, rock, colours, light and time of day ({time}), so the two views match each other. Natural light, everything at game scale; no studio, no backdrop, no frame, no people, no labels, no text. {style} reference for a 3D game's procedural environment, seen from above and from inside.
two-panel.author: Capture each panel's camera from the game (left panel: view 0, right panel: view 1), each at half the reference's width and its full height, and join them side by side in the same order with a thin dark line between them (tools/studio/shot-sheet.mjs --bare --cols 2 --width <reference width>). That one picture is the round's capture.
review: One reference picture, two panels of the same landform: compare the capture panel by panel (left with left, right with right), and check that both panels show the same landform.
Write notes per view: start each line of 'wrong' with the view's name (for example 'Aerial overview:' or 'Player's eye:'), and name each view in the summary.
Give one score for the whole picture: both views count; a view that is missing, or framed as a studio object, holds the score at most 2.

flag.rule: A stored reference for an asset whose class is not object, made from the studio wording (its prompt starts 'Studio photo of' or says 'neutral grey backdrop', or its file is named studio-photo-...), is flagged 'needs new reference'. It is kept, never deleted or replaced by itself; only the owner's Make new reference or the tab's new_reference action for a flagged reference replaces it, keeping the old one as a backup. Scores are never changed.

staging.about: Attribute assets (the owner, 2026-11-11: "for distant fog, we need simple shapes ... the recipe that we're generating is about the fog, and not about grass or a hedgerow or trees"; "as part of the reference prompt the instructions should be to the reviewer as to what they are to focus on"). An asset that is a PROPERTY of the world rather than a thing in it, an air visual effect (the owner, 2026-11-11: "Fog, smoke, steam, haze, gas these are all types of air visual effects"; "In visual effects (VFX), fog and smoke fall under FX (Effects), specifically within the sub-discipline of volumetric simulation or fluid dynamics"; distance fog first) is shown on neutral staging: plain grey blocks on flat grey ground, so nothing but the property changes across the picture. It is set by hand per asset with `staging` in catalog/procedural/library.json (never guessed); it works for any class, and the asset keeps its class (and with it its triangle budget and the server's checks), and its own `staged` entry in `assets` holds the staged framing, the reviewer's focus and its subject. The focus travels with the prompt: it is stored with the reference picture (review_focus) and with the owner's saved prompt (focus), and the reviewer's brief reads it from there first. A stored picture of a staged asset whose prompt lacks the marker is flagged 'needs new reference' (why 'staging'); that flag never pauses a running column, the new picture applies from the next round.

isolated.template: {lead} {what} shown alone on neutral staging: {show}. Camera at a standing player's eye height (1.7 m), {aim}, {fov} degree horizontal field of view, horizon {horizon}. {time}. The staging is only plain matte mid-grey blocks and pillars on flat, featureless mid-grey ground, all one untextured material, so that nothing in the picture changes from near to far except the {attribute}; no grass, no plants, no trees, no hedges, no hills, no rocks, no buildings, no water, no people, no text. {style} reference for a 3D game's procedural {attribute}, on neutral attribute staging.
isolated.author: Capture the round in the dev scene `fogstage` (feature fogstage of examples/proc-field; kit.proc_field.fogstage_view 0, the reference view): the same grey blocks on flat grey ground at near, middle and far distance from eye height, with your fog on. Change only the fog; never add terrain, grass, trees or textures to the staging.
review: ATTRIBUTE ON NEUTRAL STAGING: score only the named attribute ({focus}). The grey blocks, pillars and ground are staging: their shape, number, placement, material, texture and edges are never scored, never a 'wrong' line, a Blocker or a fix.
Light and sky count only where the {attribute} changes them (its glow, its colour at the horizon).

The capture must use the same staging (grey blocks on flat grey ground at near, middle and far distance) from the reference's eye-height camera and horizon; a capture on other scenery (terrain, grass, trees) scores at most 2, however good its {attribute}, because it can't be compared like for like.
